rows.item: “How to use this book” (a heading with no text under it)
rows.note: The draft had only the heading, so the section was written: what a translator does, the four steps, the journey through the parts and how each chapter guides you.

rows.item: Definitions: “Principles = Foundations”
rows.note: A bare one-line gloss with no context or explanation.

rows.item: Translation = transferring or conveying meanings; “an activity or process of transferring textual meaning from one language to another” (given at the start and again in the translator section)
rows.where: Chapter 1, Step 1; Words to remember, Chapter 1
rows.note: Kept as a quotation credited to the course materials, next to Newmark (1988); the key term now treats written translation ({{الترجمة التحريرية}}) as the narrow sense.

rows.item: Abbreviations TS, SL, TL, SLC and TLC, with Arabic ({{لغة المصدر}}, {{لغة الهدف}}, {{علم الترجمة}})
rows.note: All five are in the list at the back, with Arabic added for SLC and TLC and the Arabic wording adjusted; the chapters themselves say “source text” and “target text”.

rows.item: Empty labels: Interpretation, Form, Meaning, Intralingual, Interlingual
rows.where: Words to remember, Chapters 1 and 5; Chapter 27, Step 1
rows.note: The draft gave only the labels, so short definitions were written for interpreting, form and meaning; intralingual and interlingual appear as kinds of subtitles.

rows.item: Idiom definition: “a structure of more than one word whose total meaning is not the sum of its words”, with “It’s a piece of cake”
rows.where: Chapter 9, Step 1; Words to remember, Chapter 9
rows.note: Kept, but the draft gave it three times, so the copies were merged; a note on frozen words and how to spot an idiom was added.

rows.item: Literal translation, also called “modified literal translation” ({{ترجمة حرفية معدلة}})
rows.note: Kept as the key-term definition, with the Arabic written {{الترجمة الحرفية المعدّلة}}; the second copy was merged.

rows.item: Language structure note: “Arabic is a compositional (derivational) language, whereas English is a compounding language”
rows.note: An oversimplification, because both languages use derivation and compounding.

rows.item: English is SVO and Arabic is VSO; “when translating from English to Arabic we start with the verb”; the table example “Sam ate the cake” ({{سام اكل التفاحة}} marked wrong, {{اكل سام التفاحة}} marked right); “In Arabic start with the verb” ({{جملة فعلية}}, Exercise 26)
rows.where: Chapter 4, Step 1; Words to remember, Chapter 4
rows.note: Softened: formal Arabic often starts with the verb, but a sentence that starts with the subject is also correct; the Arabic now matches the English (cake, not apple).

rows.item: Table rows: sentence length (English short, Arabic long and joined by commas) and use of synonyms (Arabic uses two synonyms side by side for emphasis)
rows.where: Chapter 4, Steps 1 and 4; Chapter 14, Step 2; Chapter 23, Step 3
rows.note: Both kept as tendencies, not rules, with {{شجاعٌ مِغوار}} → “very brave” as the example.

rows.item: Table row: language formality (formal vs informal, drama and dialogue often informal); Types of Arabic: Classical, Standard, Dialectal
rows.where: Chapter 4, Step 5; Words to remember, Chapter 4; Chapter 19, Step 4; Chapter 27, Step 3
rows.note: Merged into advice on register and dialect: Modern Standard Arabic is the usual choice for written translation, and a dialect only when the client, audience or medium calls for it.

rows.item: Common challenges: grammar ({{نحو}}), semantics (choice of words), punctuation and style, general vs technical text
rows.note: Kept as four groups; “semantics” is now called word choice ({{اختيار المفردات}}) and formality is named register.

rows.item: Table Ex. 1: “He is in bed” → {{نائم}}; “As an officer” / “As a Manager of the Company” → {{بصفتي}}; “Shops stay open”; “Eventually” → {{في نهاية المطاف}}; “to see the Roman ruins”
rows.note: All kept with the Arabic completed and the trap explained; for example “in bed” is now {{إنه في فراشه}} or {{إنه نائم}} depending on context, and “I” was added to the “as” examples.

rows.item: Note on nouns with no feminine form: {{قاضي}}, {{نائب}}, {{ضابط}} ({{قاضية}} and {{نائبة}} have other meanings)
rows.note: Kept for {{قاضية}} and {{نائبة}}, with the added note that both are widely used today for women judges and members of parliament; {{ضابط}} was dropped from this note.

rows.item: “is” → {{تعد}}, with the note {{تعد الترجمة تخصصاً / مجالاً / موضوعاً مثيراً للاهتمام}} (repeated in Exercise 26 as {{يعد الطقس متقلب…}} and “copular” verbs)
rows.note: Corrected: in the present tense Arabic normally leaves out “is”, and {{تُعدّ}} (“is considered”) is only an option in formal writing when the sentence gives an opinion.

rows.item: Objectives of the book: the basic rules and principles; the differences ({{الاختلافات}}); the difficulties ({{الصعوبات}}); strategies and techniques ({{الحلول}})
rows.note: Kept as the list “By the end of it, you should…”, with a fifth aim added (check your own work and explain your choices).

rows.item: Characteristics of a translator (bilingual knowledge; cultural knowledge equal to linguistic knowledge); Skills of the translator (fluent in both languages, encyclopedic knowledge, aware of the topic, experience); Key skills (walking encyclopedia, linguistic repertoire, mental lexicon, bilingual, bicultural, idiomaticity)
rows.note: Three overlapping lists were merged into five plain points, with a quotation from al-Jāḥiẓ added; the technical labels were not kept.

rows.item: Translation as interlingual communication; “communication means to understand and to be understood”; the elements sender, receiver, channel, message, perceived value and noise
rows.note: Technical theory for beginners; the idea is kept in plain words: your reader must understand the translation.

rows.item: Intralingual vs interlingual communication (paraphrasing inside one language)
rows.note: Reworded: rewording a text in the same language is a kind of translation in a wider sense (Jakobson, 1959), but the handbook focuses on translating between two languages.

rows.item: Process of translation (paragraph → sentences → phrases → words; cause-and-effect links); General tips: fidelity ({{الأمانة}}), revise, faithful and accurate and acceptable, translation is rewriting, the minefield ({{الترجمة كانه حقل الألغام}}), prose vs poetry
rows.where: Chapter 2, “While you translate” and “After you translate”; Chapter 1, Step 4
rows.note: All kept as practical tips; the poetry point is reworded (poetry allows more creative freedom, informative texts must be exact) and “rewriting” appears as understanding first, then writing again.

rows.item: A different definition: translation as approximation, mainly of cultural meaning
rows.where: Chapter 1, Step 2; Words to remember, Chapter 1; Chapter 15
rows.note: Kept as “approximation”, supported by Eco (2003); the link to culture is developed in the chapter on cultural approximation.

rows.item: “Translation also means to politicize ({{الدبلوماسية}})”, for example asking your father for money in a persuasive way
rows.note: Persuasive wording is not a definition of translation, and the Arabic word given does not match “politicize”.

rows.item: “In translation we have our own jargon” (Terminology and jargon)
rows.note: The one-line remark is covered by the chapter on special terms; translation terms are explained in each chapter’s Words to remember.

rows.item: Translator types: commissioned (a client asks you; must follow their ideology and policy) and self-initiated (you choose your own text, no clients)
rows.where: Chapter 1, Step 5; Words to remember, Chapter 1
rows.note: Kept with plain definitions; freelance and in-house translators are explained as doing commissioned work.

rows.item: Client ideology example: “A suicide bomber killed 10 Israelis” → {{انتحاري}} (“UnIslamic ideology”) / {{استشهادي}} (“Islamic ideology”)
rows.note: Rewritten neutrally: {{انتحاري}} matches the English, {{استشهادي}} adds praise, so follow the client’s policy; the nationality of the victims and the religious labels were removed.

rows.item: Equivalence: the three types (formal, functional, ideational) listed in three places; “a central concept of Translation Studies”; “translation seeks to establish equivalence between two languages at different levels”; the definition of each type
rows.where: Chapter 10, Step 1; Words to remember, Chapter 10
rows.note: The repeated lists were merged into one chapter and credited to Farghal & Shunnaq; the statements about a central concept and “different levels” were not kept.

rows.item: “The agreement remained dead letter since then”: formal ({{حرفاً ميتاً}}), functional ({{حبراً على ورق}}) and ideational versions; treaty ({{معاهدة}}) vs agreement ({{اتفاقية}})
rows.where: Chapter 10, Step 1; Try it, Chapter 10; Chapter 14, Step 1; Chapter 25, Step 4
rows.note: Same three versions, with the English corrected to “has remained a dead letter” and the ideational Arabic changed from {{المعاهدة}} to {{الاتفاقية}} to match “agreement”; the treaty and agreement difference is a one-line note.

rows.item: “You should think outside the box” (formal {{فكر خارج الصندوق}}; {{فكر بتفكير خلاق / إبداعياً}}); “Ali is second to none in writing poetry” (functional {{لا يشق له غبار}}; ideational {{متميز}})
rows.where: Chapter 10, Step 2; Try it, Chapter 10; Chapter 14, Step 1
rows.note: The plain “think creatively” version is now labelled ideational, and the ideational version of the poetry sentence is now {{لا يُضاهى}}, because {{متميز}} does not say “second to none”.

rows.item: Rule: meaning over form ({{عند المترجمين المعنى أهم من البناء}}); form = {{البناء}} (a clause, sentence, word structure and so on); “behind any form there is meaning”; you can change the form but not the meaning
rows.where: Chapter 5, Step 1; Words to remember, Chapter 5
rows.note: Kept, with the repeated statements merged; the Arabic word for form is now {{الشكل}}, and Nida & Taber (1969) is cited for the principle.

rows.item: Structural adjustment: change an adjective into a verb, or a verb into a noun
rows.note: Kept with new examples: “He is a heavy smoker” → {{يدخّن بشراهة}} and “after his arrival” → {{بعد أن وصل}}.

rows.item: “Blair: Bush’s puppy” → {{منقاد لبوش}} / {{تابع لبوش}} / “{{حروف}} or {{غنمة}}”, presented as a clearer example that form is more important than meaning
rows.note: “Puppy” was corrected to “poodle” and explained; the two neutral Arabic options are kept, the informal animal words are left out, and the example now shows keeping the meaning and changing the form.

rows.item: “Why is meaning complex? Because it is cognitive (intellectual and abstract)”
rows.note: Theory that a beginner cannot use.

rows.item: Denotation and connotation: definitions (core meaning vs shades of meaning), given twice; labels {{المعنى اللغوي / المعنى الحرفي}} and {{المعنى اصطلاحاً}}; “two semantic labels”
rows.where: Chapter 6, Step 1; Words to remember, Chapter 6
rows.note: The two copies were merged; the Arabic labels are now {{المعنى المعجمي}} and {{المعنى الإيحائي}}, and Baker’s (2018) terms propositional and expressive meaning were added.

rows.item: Denotative “Died = {{قتل}}” and connotative “Died = {{استشهد}}”; die / pass away / kick the bucket (“died in a good way / a bad way”); “Kick the bucket = {{يموت كالحقير}}” in the strategies list
rows.note: The Arabic was corrected: {{مات}} is neutral and {{تُوُفِّي}} is polite; “kick the bucket” is described as informal and humorous, and the insulting Arabic and {{استشهد}} are not used.

rows.item: steed = {{جواد}}, horse = {{حصان}}, mule = {{بغل}}; comrade: denotation {{صديق}}, connotation {{رفيق}} (same party)
rows.note: Steed and horse are kept, and mule was dropped because it is a different animal; comrade is kept as friend (general) against comrade (same party or cause).

rows.item: Kill ({{قتل}}) vs assassinated ({{اغتيال}})
rows.note: The two words differ in meaning, not only in feeling, so they do not show connotation well.

rows.item: Sentence meaning vs speaker’s meaning: {{أشعر بالحر}} (turn on the air conditioning), {{أصبح الجو بارداً}} (turn it off)
rows.where: Chapter 6, Step 2; Words to remember, Chapter 6
rows.note: Both Arabic examples are kept, with an English example added and plain English definitions instead of the Arabic labels.

rows.item: Collocation: “the company a word keeps”; pay money / pay attention / pay respect / pay a visit
rows.where: Chapter 8, Step 1; Words to remember, Chapter 8
rows.note: The two copies were merged and the definition is quoted from the course materials, linked to Firth (1957); the Arabic was corrected (for example {{ينتبه}} or {{يُعير انتباهه}}, and the wrong {{يدفع زيارة}} is shown).

rows.item: Close cooperation = {{تعاون وثيق}}; close friend = {{صديق مقرب}}
rows.note: Same examples and Arabic, now inside a list of English-to-Arabic collocations.

rows.item: Arabic examples: {{استل سيفه}}, {{يساورني القلق}}
rows.note: English translations were added (“he drew his sword”, “I am worried”), with three more Arabic-to-English examples.

rows.item: Context: definition (background information that helps us understand a text); “in translation pay attention to context”; micro context (co-text) vs macro context (audience, author such as {{أحمد شوقي}} / {{نزار قباني}} / {{محمود درويش}}, translator, time and place); “Every communicative situation has its own context” ({{لكل مقام مقال}}); the translation triangle (text, translator, audience, author)
rows.where: Chapter 7, Steps 1–2; Words to remember, Chapter 7
rows.note: The confusing two-column table was rewritten as “look near, then look far”, with Arabic terms; the triangle is described in words with the translator in the middle, and Ahmad Shawqi was dropped from the authors.

rows.item: Homonymy vs polysemy: definitions; examples {{عين}} (spy / eye / spring), {{تطهير}} (sins / wound), {{احتجاز}} (water / hostages); “case” (situation, issue, cover of a mobile, container) and “bank” ({{مؤسسة مالية}} / {{ضفة النهر}})
rows.where: Chapter 7, Step 3; Words to remember, Chapter 7
rows.note: Kept in the context chapter, because context decides which meaning is right; {{التطهير من الذنوب}} is written in full, “cover of a mobile” became a glasses case, and {{خط}} was added.

rows.item: Polysemy example {{بناء}} ({{العمارة بناء}} / {{الكلية بناء}})
rows.note: Left out for space; the other examples show the point.

rows.item: Rule: an idiom “cannot be translated denotationally”
rows.note: Softened to “do not translate an idiom word by word unless the other language has the same idiom”, and five ways to translate an idiom (Baker, 2018) were added.

rows.item: “It’s raining cats and dogs” → {{تمطر بغزارة}}; “over the moon” → {{في قمة السعادة}}; “I am all ears” → {{كلي آذان صاغية}}; {{كالمستجير من الرمضاء بالنار}} = “out of the frying pan into the fire”
rows.where: Chapter 9, Steps 3–4; Chapter 2 (first translation); Chapter 22, Step 3
rows.note: Same Arabic and English pairs; the raining idiom is also the worked example in Chapter 2 and the machine-translation example in Chapter 22.

rows.item: “To pull one’s socks up” → {{شمر عن ساعديه}}; “A piece of cake” ({{سهل}} vs {{قطعة من الكعك}}); “to be in the red” → {{مديون}}
rows.note: The English became “to roll up one’s sleeves” (the Arabic literally means this), “a piece of cake” now has the context that decides its meaning, and “in the red” is {{يعاني عجزاً مالياً}}.

rows.item: “Idiom: more than two words that have a special meaning”: to pay a visit ({{يقوم بزيارة}} right, {{يدفع زيارة}} wrong); strong tea ({{شاي ثقيل}} right, {{شاي قوي}} wrong)
rows.note: Reclassified as collocations, not idioms, and moved to the collocation chapter.

rows.item: “Article 12 – Governing Law” → {{القانون المطبق}} (right) / {{القانون الحاكم}} (wrong); Article = {{المادة}} in a constitution, {{البند}} in an agreement
rows.note: Now an entry in a term list: {{القانون الواجب التطبيق}} comes first, {{القانون المطبَّق}} is an alternative and {{القانون الحاكم}} is called a common calque, not wrong.

rows.item: mocktail and cocktail (non-alcoholic and alcoholic drinks in the West); “warmed my heart” = {{أثلج صدري}} (winter has a good connotation in the Arab region)
rows.where: Chapter 15, Steps 2–3; Try it, Chapter 15; Chapter 24, Step 2
rows.note: “Mocktail” is kept with {{مشروب مُنعش بلا كحول}} and “cocktail” was dropped; “warmed my heart” is a full sentence, explained by relief and joy being linked with coolness in a hot climate.

rows.item: Literal translation “can be either successful or destructive” ({{قد تكون الترجمة الحرفية إما ناجحة أو مدمرة}}): pay a visit → {{يدفع زيارة}} (no equivalent), play a role → {{يلعب دوراً}} (equivalent); “It has been a long day” ({{يوماً شاقاً}} right, {{يوماً طويلاً}} wrong); “What are you wearing on your biggest day?” ({{ماذا سترتدي في يوم زفافك}} right)
rows.where: Chapter 11, Step 1; Try it, Chapter 11; Chapter 19, Step 2
rows.note: Merged with free translation in one chapter; all examples kept, with the reason for “long day” added (in English a long day is a tiring one) and the wedding-advert context for “biggest day”.

rows.item: Metaphoric translation: metaphor (“she is a moon”) vs simile (“she is beautiful like a moon”); figurative language ({{اللغة المجازية}}); metaphor defined in English and in Arabic; “in poetry language is very expressive and impressive”
rows.where: Chapter 12, Steps 1–2; Words to remember, Chapter 12
rows.note: Definitions kept, but the moon examples were replaced by “He is a lion” and “He is as brave as a lion”, the Arabic definition was replaced by the Arabic rhetoric view ({{تشبيه بليغ}}, {{استعارة}}), and the poetry line became “Poetry is especially rich in metaphors”.

rows.item: Three techniques: shared metaphor → translate literally (“she is a snake” → {{إنها أفعى}}); not shared → another metaphor ({{إنها كالثعلب}}); no equivalent → the basic meaning ({{إنها خطيرة أو خبيثة}}), “the worst choice”
rows.note: The order is kept and a fourth option (turn it into a simile) was added; the snake example is used only for the shared image, with other examples for the rest.

rows.item: Examples: “the tip of the iceberg” ({{غيض من فيض}} / {{أول الغيث قطرة}} / {{وما خفي أعظم}}); “raises the brows” → {{تُصدم}}; “My paper will see light next December”; “My thoughts evaporate” → {{تبخرت أفكاري}}
rows.note: {{غيضٌ من فيض}} and {{وما خفي كان أعظم}} are kept and {{أول الغيث قطرة}} was dropped because it means that big things start small; the other three were corrected to “raised a few eyebrows”, “see the light of day” and “My hopes evaporated”.

rows.item: Keywords “Rhetoric = {{البلاغة}}”, “Poetic = {{فصيح او جزل}}”; table Subjective ({{ذاتي / شخصي}}) and Objective ({{موضوعي}})
rows.note: Vocabulary notes that the technique does not need.

rows.item: Free translation: “applied to everything, not only literary works”; also called loose translation (“Ample Freedom”); some specialists see adapted translation as a new text, not a translation
rows.where: Chapter 11, Steps 2–3; Words to remember, Chapter 11
rows.note: “Loose translation” and the view that adaptation is a new text are kept as key terms; the remark that free translation applies to all texts is not made.

rows.item: Four free-translation examples: equal-opportunity appointments; heavy rainfall; “Going out can be risky these days”; parents not happy about what he said
rows.note: All four kept as examples of going too far: the appointment sentence is shown in a literal, a natural and a too-free version, and the other three are described with a warning that they add ideas.

rows.item: Literal translation, including idiomatic translation (an idiom with another idiom); “Key word” = {{كلمات مفتاحية}} (wrong) / {{كلمات دالة}} (right)
rows.note: Kept, and the key-word example is now advice to check the field, because either Arabic term can be right.

rows.item: “Most of the time, literal translation fails”
rows.note: The handbook shows many successful literal translations (for example “to play a role” and shared metaphors), so the general claim was not kept.

rows.item: “Kick the chair” = {{انتحر}}
rows.note: Could not be confirmed as an established English idiom.

rows.item: Functional translation (translation of equivalents): “spill the beans” = {{يفشي السر}}; “mark my words” = {{فل تتذكر وعدي / كلامي}}
rows.note: Both are kept but now shown as giving the plain meaning; “mark my words” is corrected to {{تذكّر كلامي}}, and the functional examples became “a dead letter” and “second to none”.

rows.item: Cultural substitution: “They are like Romeo and Juliet” = {{هما كقيس وليلى}}
rows.note: Same example, used for adaptation in Chapter 13 and for cultural substitution in Chapter 14.

rows.item: Addition (English to Arabic; “Arabic is a language of elaboration”, {{اسهاب}}); Omission (Arabic to English; “when we want to be polite”; {{شجاع ومغوار}} = “brave and daring” wrong, “brave or quite brave” right)
rows.where: Chapter 14, Step 2; Chapter 4, Step 4; Chapter 23, Step 3
rows.note: Addition now says that Arabic style often favours fuller expression ({{الإطناب}}) and readers may need extra information; omission is corrected to {{شجاعٌ مِغوار}} → “very brave”, with a warning never to omit real information.

rows.item: Explanatory translation: “the last option”, for cultural words and technical terms ({{الحرمان}}, {{العدة}}, {{الزكاة}}, {{الصدقة}}; repeated under Descriptive Translation)
rows.note: “The last option” became “use it only when nothing shorter works”; {{الزكاة}} and {{العِدّة}} are kept, and {{الحرمان}} and {{الصدقة}} were dropped.

rows.item: “Arabicization is a form of naturalization”; Exercise 27: transliterated form (loan word), {{الاستعارة الصوتية}}, “Radio” → {{الراديو}}
rows.note: Kept under transliteration as Arabicisation ({{التعريب}}), with radio → {{الراديو}} and two more examples; the key term uses the Arabic {{النقل الصوتي}} (Chapter 16).

rows.item: “Terms ({{مصطلحات}}) convey complex meaning (a concept)”; “every branch of linguistics has its own terms”; “terms categorise the text”; “concept = complex meaning” ({{مفهوم}}); “the translator sometimes works as a coiner”
rows.where: Chapter 21, Steps 1 and 3; Words to remember, Chapter 16; Chapter 17, Step 1; Chapter 19, Step 4
rows.note: Merged into the terminology and lexical creation chapters; “concept” is now defined as an idea that a word or term stands for, and the coiner idea is kept in plain words.

rows.item: “The Jordanian Academy of the Arabic Language has 74 specialised Arabicised fields” ({{مجمع اللغة العربية الأردني}})
rows.note: The figure could not be verified; the academies, including the one in Amman, are named in Chapter 21.

rows.item: Exercise 24: {{حقل مخضوضر / مائل للخضرة}} (a greenish field)
rows.note: Kept as one suffix example: greenish → {{مائل إلى الخضرة}}.

rows.item: Exercise 25: “fast colour” → {{لون ثابت}} ({{ثبات الألوان}}); “fast friend” = {{صديق وفي / صديق العمر}}; {{قهوة خفيفة}}; {{بحر هائج / مائج}}
rows.note: “Fast colour” is used twice (as a collocation and as the dictionary three-check example); the draft gave only the Arabic for {{قهوة خفيفة}} and {{بحر هائج}}, so the English (“weak coffee”, “a rough sea”) was added.

rows.item: Exercise 25 and Exercise 16: “breaching” = {{خرق}}, “to be in breach of law”, {{كسر القانون}} vs {{مخالفة القانون}}; “Break the rules” → {{خرق القواعد}} / {{مخالفة}} / {{تجاوز}}
rows.note: Reduced to one point: “break the law” is more natural as {{يخالف القانون}} than {{يكسر القانون}}.

rows.item: Exercises 24, 25 and 26, items not used: “a readable book”, “a conceivable resolution”, {{ممتلكات قابلة للاسترجاع}}, {{قضية جدلية}}, {{سلوك صبياني}}; “addled egg”, {{قميص سادة}} (plain / plains), “cover news”; {{هذه حديقة غناء}}, {{لاذ اللص بالفرار}}, “Sounds great” → {{تبدو جيدة}}, {{تمتلك عالمة مقومات الزوجة الصالحة}}
rows.note: Left out for space; the draft notes are brief and do not explain the point of each item.

rows.item: Approximation and cultural approximation (to bring the meaning as close as possible; needs cultural knowledge of both languages)
rows.where: Chapter 15, Step 1; Words to remember, Chapter 15
rows.note: Kept and explained through the idea “translate the feeling, not the picture”, citing Farghal & Shunnaq.

rows.item: “I have got the test in the bag” → {{الامتحان في جيبي}}; “Like mother, like daughter” → {{اقلب الجرة على فمها…}}; “cut from the same cloth” → {{علي واحمد اثنين من نفس الطينة}}
rows.note: Kept with informal and formal options marked (for example {{النجاح في الامتحان مضمون}}), and the “same cloth” Arabic corrected to {{عليّ وأحمد من طينةٍ واحدة}}.

rows.item: “As busy as a bee” → {{زي أم العروس}}; “Scapegoating” → {{كبش الفداء}} / {{حطها برقبتي}} / {{حطها بوجعي}}; “sleep like a log” (four Arabic options)
rows.note: The colloquial Arabic was replaced by one standard expression each: {{نشيطٌ كالنحلة}}, {{كبش فداء}} and {{نام كالقتيل}}.

rows.item: “Death is the great leveller” = {{كل نفس ذائقة الموت}}
rows.note: A Qur’anic verse should not be used as a translation equivalent here.

rows.item: “Big sins” = {{الكبائر}} (Exercise 28); “Every jack must have his jill” = {{لكل روح توأمه}}
rows.note: Left out for space.

rows.item: “Jet lag” = {{إعياء الطيران}}
rows.note: Moved to the strategies chapter as an example of paraphrase, with the Arabic changed to {{الإرهاق الناتج عن فارق التوقيت}}.

rows.item: UK and US offices: the Home Office → {{وزير الداخلية}}, the Chancellor of the Exchequer and the Secretary of the Treasury → {{وزير المالية}}, the Secretary of State → {{وزير الخارجية}}; “The British Home Office” (Exercise 28); sheriff; watchdog press vs lapdog press
rows.note: Merged into one set with the country named in each item; the Home Office is now a ministry ({{وزارة}}), the Treasury post is {{وزير الخزانة}}, sheriff is {{رئيس شرطة المقاطعة}}, and the press terms are {{الصحافة الرقابية}} and {{الصحافة الموالية}}.

rows.item: “Minister of Foreign Affairs or Minister of Exterior (in Kuwait)”; “sometimes ‘Department’ means {{وزارة}}”
rows.note: The UK and US examples already make the point about titles.

rows.item: The Republican “House Managers” at President Clinton’s impeachment trial → {{المحامون المعينون لمجلس الشيوخ الجمهوري}}; intern; scandal
rows.note: It is about a political scandal involving a named person, and it was not needed to show the point.

rows.item: Exercise 29: “God willing” = {{إن شاء الله}}; “We are well” = {{الحمد لله}}; condolences {{تعيش انت، شعبان مات}}; welcome {{أهلاً أهلاً زارنا النبي}}
rows.note: The first two are kept (the second made fuller: {{الحمد لله، بخير}}); the two colloquial phrases were replaced by {{عظّم الله أجركم}} (formal, with {{البقية في حياتك}} marked Egyptian) and {{أهلاً وسهلاً، شرّفتمونا}}.

rows.item: Exercise 29: “What the hell are you talking” = {{اتق الله يا شيخ}}; “Calm down, take it easy” = {{وحدوا الله والمسامح كريم}}
rows.note: Colloquial and not suitable for a general handbook.

rows.item: Product cannibalism ({{منتج يزاحم منتجاً آخر}}; literal meaning about eating human flesh)
rows.note: The term became “product cannibalisation”, with a one-line explanation in Arabic and English, and the literal-meaning line was dropped.

rows.item: Descriptive translation: an explanatory strategy that paraphrases a source expression by describing it conceptually (also called explanatory translation, {{الترجمة الشرحية}}); the first step is to transliterate, e.g. “zakat”; the description goes in brackets or in a footnote
rows.where: Chapter 16, Step 1; Try it and Words to remember, Chapter 16
rows.note: The two copies (here and under lexical creation) were merged and set out as three steps: transliterate, describe, and describe only the first time.

rows.item: {{زكاة}} (“compulsory charity when income conditions are met”; “an Islamic taxation system… annually”); {{تيمم}} (“making ablutions with earth when water is scarce”)
rows.note: Both kept with corrected descriptions: zakat is a fixed share of savings and wealth above a minimum, not income, and “Islamic taxation system” was dropped; tayammum is dry ritual purification with clean earth.

rows.item: {{الحوقلة}}, {{البسملة}}, {{التأريخ}}, {{القهقهة}}, {{القرقرة}} ({{أشد درجات الضحك}})
rows.note: {{البسملة}} and {{الحوقلة}} are kept with short descriptions (and the blending of {{بسم الله}} is explained in Chapter 17); the other three were dropped because the draft gives no explanation of them.

rows.item: “Sectioning”: “Ali has been sectioned” → hospitalised in a psychiatric clinic, treated and discharged (given twice)
rows.note: Kept once, with the Arabic corrected to {{أُودِع عليٌّ مستشفى للأمراض النفسية بموجب القانون}} and the draft’s spelling errors removed.

rows.item: “Atwah” = {{عطوة}}, a three-month truce ({{هدنة}}) in Jordanian culture
rows.note: Moved here as “a temporary truce in tribal customary law, for example in Jordan”; the three-month detail was dropped.

rows.item: Vocabulary notes: “Dust” = {{غبار / تراب}}; “peace talk” = {{المفاوضات}}; “columnist” = {{من كتاب الأعمدة}}; “subordination” = {{تبعية}}; keywords “substitutes” = {{بدائل}}, “lexical items” = words, {{التعابير الاصطلاحية}}, “bereavement” / “bereaved families” = {{العائلات الثكلى}}
rows.note: Vocabulary notes, not examples of a technique.

rows.item: Lexical creation ({{النحت المعجمي}}): coining new lexical items by using existing words or literal translation; “the deliberate coinage of new words for culture-specific, technical or conceptual items”; why it matters (a gap in the target language)
rows.where: Chapter 17, Step 1; Words to remember, Chapter 17
rows.note: Kept; the Arabic name is now {{التوليد المعجمي}}, and {{النحت}} is explained separately as blending words into one.

rows.item: Types of lexical creation: neologism, loan translation (calque), transliteration, explanation, hybrid form
rows.note: All five kept, each defined and illustrated; “neologism” now also covers an old word given a new meaning.

rows.item: Shadow government ({{حكومة الظل}}); Thanksgiving ({{عيد الشكر}}); smartphone ({{الهاتف الذكي}}), as loan translations
rows.note: Same examples, grouped under loan translation (calque); “shadow government” is also the calque example in Chapter 13.

rows.item: Blog → {{مدونة}} (neologism); cyber security → {{الأمن السيبراني}} (“transliteration and partly Arabicised”); green washing → {{التضليل البيئي}}
rows.note: Blog is explained as coming from {{دوّن}}, cybersecurity is now the example of a hybrid form, and greenwashing is the example of an explanation.

rows.item: Hybrid form: CD = {{دسك مدمج}}; co-wife = {{الضرة}}
rows.note: Left out for space.

rows.item: Valentine’s Day = {{عيد الحب}}, listed as a loan translation
rows.note: It is not a loan translation, so it does not fit the type it was listed under.

rows.item: “To be lexicalized”: {{التعجيم}} (adding a new word to the dictionary, officially)
rows.note: The Arabic was corrected to {{المَعْجَمة}}, and the meaning is now “widely accepted and entered in the dictionary”, not “official”.

rows.item: Transliteration: “Wakf” = {{وقف}}, “Sukok” = {{صكوك}}, “AL-Istitaba” = {{الاستتابة}}
rows.where: Chapter 17, Step 2 (sukuk); Chapter 14, Step 4 and Chapter 16, Try it (waqf)
rows.note: Sukuk is kept with a definition and waqf appears in the two chapters where it fits better; {{الاستتابة}} is not used.

rows.item: {{الخلوة الشرعية}} ({{النظرة}}), “Islamically approved private exclusion”; Yin-Yang; psychology ({{علم النفس}}) vs psychiatry
rows.note: Specialist terms from other fields, left out for space.

rows.item: Coined words: “tribocracy” ({{العشائر قراطية}}), “dictatocracy”, “puppycracy”, “patriocracy”
rows.note: Made-up words rather than established terms, so they are poor models for beginners.

rows.item: Cancel culture ({{ثقافة الإلغاء}} and other options); “global warming” = {{احترار أرضي}}; “greenhouse effect” = {{احتباس حراري}}
rows.note: Used as examples of accepted terms, with one Arabic form for “cancel culture” and “global warming” corrected to {{الاحترار العالمي}}.

rows.item: Key vocabulary: translation = {{الترجمة التحريرية}}; interpretation = {{الترجمة الشفهية}}; “Provided that” = {{شريطة أن / بشرط}}
rows.where: Words to remember, Chapter 1; Chapter 21, Step 4
rows.note: Translation is now the general word with written translation as its narrower sense, and “provided that” is a term-list entry that gives only {{شريطةَ أن}}.

rows.item: “boys are boys” = {{الولد ولد لو أنه قاضي بلد}}
rows.note: Left out for space.

rows.item: “Business is Business” = {{العمل التجاري عمل تجاري}} / {{الشغل شغل}}
rows.note: Kept with the informal {{الشغل شغل}}; the literal {{العمل التجاري عمل تجاري}} is not used.

rows.item: Exercise 16: “Don’t put words on me” → {{لا تتقول علي الأقاويل}}; “To hit the sac” → {{أن يأوي إلى الفراش}}; “To break a leg” → {{أن تكون محظوظاً}}
rows.note: The English was corrected (“Don’t put words in my mouth”, “hit the sack”) and the Arabic shortened; “Break a leg!” → {{بالتوفيق!}} now opens Chapter 1.

rows.item: Analysing a text: to analyse means breaking down and processing the text; “a text is anything written: a word, a sentence or a paragraph”
rows.where: Chapter 18, Step 1; Words to remember, Chapter 18
rows.note: The definition of text was widened to any written or spoken piece of language that forms a complete message.

rows.item: Why analyse: highlight new words to work faster; identify style, strategies, length and genre; form a mental draft; each new reading brings new ideas; know the publisher; break the text into segments; “simplicity is key”; the three-step process analysis → translation → commentary
rows.where: Chapter 18, Step 1; Chapter 2, “Next: get to know the text”; Chapter 25
rows.note: Kept as a list of benefits; marking difficult words, the mental draft and “keep it simple” also appear in Chapter 2, and the third step has its own chapter.

rows.item: Assurance checklist: speaker or author, terms, field, publisher, tone, style of writing, strategies, target audience
rows.note: Kept as eight questions, with genre and purpose added.

rows.item: Worked example on a KUNA report: tone straightforward; field political; purpose (Australia); who wrote and published it; formal language; audience interested in the Middle East or Kuwait; strategy literal because there are no metaphors
rows.note: Kept as a worked analysis; “purpose: Australia” became relations between Kuwait and Australia, and genre and purpose were added.

rows.item: “KUNA has biased views”; choice-of-words examples “Government Rents” and “Linguistic Applications”
rows.note: A handbook should not describe a named organisation this way, and the word examples make no sense without the original text.

rows.item: Analysis vs summary (analysis identifies features, background and main ideas; summary presents only the facts; avoid summarising)
rows.note: Same distinction, shortened.

rows.item: Characteristics of a good analyser (be a critic, create your own model, improve proficiency and quality); “the analysis should align with your translation”; “mention issues and problems in the analysis”
rows.note: Merged into four points, including matching the translation to the analysis and noting problems for the commentary.

rows.item: Examples of word choice: Persian Gulf vs Arabian Gulf; “It’s raining cats and dogs”
rows.where: Chapter 24, Step 2; Chapter 2, “Your first translation, step by step”
rows.note: The Gulf names became an example of sensitive names (follow the client’s policy), and the idiom is the first worked translation.

rows.item: Objectives: improve critical skills and rational thinking, become a good critic, critique translations
rows.note: Moved to the commentary chapter: a commentary sharpens your reasoning and helps you judge translations.

rows.item: “Post-editing is now the new direction for translators around the world. You should assess translation quality.”
rows.note: Kept as a claim credited to the course materials: post-editing is a regular part of translators’ work.

rows.item: Tips: titles as short as possible; drop whatever can be omitted; no addition in titles; do your job thoroughly, including captions; protect your reputation; quality + speed = productivity
rows.where: Chapter 2, “While you translate” and “After you translate”
rows.note: Kept as tips, except “drop whatever can be omitted”, which was not kept as a separate rule because Chapter 14 warns never to omit real information.

rows.item: Commentary on translation: mention the problem and how it was solved; always use examples; use WH questions; write in the third person; “This was omitted due to its irrelevance to the target audience”
rows.note: All kept as writing rules, with the omission sentence reworded “because it is irrelevant to the target audience”.

rows.item: Commentary in two parts (reflecting on your analysis, reflecting on your translation); mention the strategies and techniques used for specific words, the dictionaries and resources, and justify your decisions
rows.note: Kept, and turned into five questions to answer for each problem (problem, solution, procedure or strategy, resource, justification), with a worked example.

rows.item: Heading “Terminology” (no text under it)
rows.note: The draft had no text here; the chapter was written from the team’s terminology material at beginner level.

rows.item: Heading “AI and Machine Translation” (no text under it)
rows.note: The draft had no text here; the chapter was written from published sources and other notes, and it uses the draft’s post-editing line.

rows.item: Heading “Glossary” (no text under it)
rows.note: Built from the Words to remember lists of all 27 chapters: 113 terms with Arabic equivalents, definitions and chapter numbers.

rows.item: Heading “Further Reading or references or index” (no text under it)
rows.note: The draft cited no sources, so a reference list of 42 entries in APA style and a five-book further reading list were made; no index was made.

source: Latest updates and thoughts (plan and recommendations)

rows.item: Organise the material so that it is consistent and cohesive, and remove repeated content within each chapter (he had collected related material from several sources)
rows.note: Done: topics the draft gave two or three times (equivalence, denotation and connotation, collocation, idioms, descriptive translation, translator skills) now appear once, in their own chapter.

rows.item: Add the strategies that are missing from the Translation Strategies chapter
rows.note: Done: explicitation and implicitation, a more general word, a more neutral word, paraphrase, loan word plus explanation, compensation, domestication and foreignisation were added.

rows.item: Add the types of translation that are missing
rows.note: Done: written translation, interpreting, sight translation, audiovisual translation and localisation (Chapter 1); literal, free, adaptation and communicative translation (Chapter 11); subtitling, dubbing, voice-over and audio description (Chapter 26).

rows.item: Add a new chapter on the seven translation procedures (asked for twice)
rows.note: Done: the seven procedures of Vinay and Darbelnet, direct and oblique procedures, and one sentence analysed with several procedures.

rows.item: Add more material to the cultural approximation chapter
rows.note: Done as far as can be told: Chapter 15 has four steps of examples, but the plan does not say what material was to be added.

rows.item: Every chapter should include definitions of its key concepts
rows.note: Done: every chapter has a Words to remember box with an Arabic equivalent and a short definition for each term.

rows.item: All key terms, minor or significant, should be in a glossary at the end of the handbook (asked several times)
rows.note: Partly: the glossary has 113 terms taken from the Words to remember boxes, but some terms explained in the text are missing, such as sight translation, localisation, direct and oblique procedures, spotting, SDH, hard and soft news, initialism, acronym, sociolect and idiolect.

rows.item: Add a chapter on machine translation and AI (Loulwah’s notes discuss machine translation; he had not yet read her notes)
rows.note: Done: the chapter covers the tools, when a machine can help, typical mistakes, post-editing and four safety rules, using the draft’s post-editing point and published sources; Loulwah’s notes on machine translation were not among the files.

rows.item: Follow what the team discussed before, go through the framework again, and cover the sections mentioned in the chat (asked three times)
rows.note: Partly: the framework document was followed (chapter list, beginner level, principles then examples), but the earlier discussions and the chat were not among the files, so they could not be checked.

rows.item: A general section or chapter of exercises at the end, with three levels of text length, practising all theories and most genres and applying the checklists
rows.note: Partly: the three-level section was written and then removed to keep the handbook short, and one final task on a press release remains.

rows.item: “You may find some useful examples in the book”
rows.note: The plan does not say which book was meant, so this could not be followed up.

rows.item: Add news texts and articles as authentic translation material; use examples from news sources (asked twice)
rows.where: Chapter 2, “Before you start”; Chapter 18, Step 4; Chapter 19, Step 3
rows.note: Partly: news is taught with headline examples and a described KUNA report, but no full published article is included.

rows.item: Extract sentences that illustrate the theories from the Analysis, 180 and 386 texts
rows.note: The texts were not received; only the description of a KUNA news report from the draft’s analysis section appears (Chapters 2 and 18).

rows.item: Include examples from poetry
rows.note: Done in a small way: a line by al-Mutanabbi and Shakespeare’s “Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day?”.

rows.item: Include the main genres, with at least one example for each genre
rows.note: Partly: eight genres are given and seven have a translated example; advertising has only a description (an advert example is in Chapter 11).

rows.item: Add a section at the beginning on tips, advice, techniques and preparation for translation ({{فصل في النصائح والتقنيات والإعداد للترجمة}})
rows.note: Done: Chapter 2 covers what to do before, during and after translating, and ends with a worked first translation.

rows.item: Include a number of practical checklists
rows.where: Chapter 18, Step 4; “The translator’s workflow”; “Translation quality checklist”; “When in doubt”
rows.note: Done as short guides: the analysis checklist, a seven-step workflow with Do and Don’t boxes, a tick-box quality checklist and a When in doubt page.

rows.item: Discuss the questions: Who is the client? What is the communication purpose? Who is the target audience?
rows.where: Chapter 2, “Before you start”; Words to remember, Chapter 2
rows.note: Done: the three questions form the translation brief (Nord, 1997), and the brief is referred to again in later chapters such as 14, 20 and 26.

rows.item: Add a chapter on terminology management and terminology guides (the terminology chapter was passed to Masooma)
rows.note: Done: the chapter is written from the team’s terminology material at beginner level, defines term list, termbase and terminology guide, and gives a sample term list.

rows.item: Include an Interlingual Risk Assessment Matrix
rows.note: Done: ten risk areas, each with an example, a risk level and what to do, supported by Pym (2015).

rows.item: Mention the audiences and materials that will be covered in future editions of the handbook
rows.note: Written, then removed to keep the handbook short.

rows.item: Anything taken from the text {{الترجمة: ماهيتها وكيفيتها}} must be cited and attributed to Dr Yusuf
rows.note: Partly: only two idioms (“He looks blue”, “I will go bananas”) were taken from it, and they are cited as the team’s course materials because the pages received carry no author or publication details.

rows.item: Add a chapter on text analysis, at the beginning, middle or end of the handbook
rows.note: Done: text analysis is presented as the first of three phases (analysis, translation, commentary), built from the draft’s section on analysing a text.

rows.item: Add a chapter on translation commentary, including how to analyse a translation and write commentary notes
rows.note: Done: two parts, five questions for each problem, rules for writing and a worked example; Chapter 18 adds that the analysis can also be used to judge a finished translation.

rows.item: Add a chapter on printed and digital dictionaries ({{المعاجم المطبوعة والرقمية}})
rows.note: Done: kinds of dictionary, the three-check rule, printed versus digital, and dictionaries to start with.

rows.item: Include Fairclough’s relational model
rows.note: Partly: the model is taught in simple words as two levels, linguistic and external (Fairclough, 2003), and as three questions in Chapter 20 (Fairclough, 1992); its technical parts were left out for beginners.

rows.item: Create three practical checklists based on Dr Abdullah’s PhD research or framework and on Fairclough’s relational model of critical discourse analysis
rows.note: Material not received: Dr Abdullah’s framework was not among the files, and no checklists based on these two were kept; Fairclough’s model appears only as questions in Chapters 18 and 20.

rows.item: Keep the Arabic version for future use
rows.note: The handbook is in English only; a note on a later Arabic version was removed together with the future-editions note.

rows.item: Shaikha to help organise the material
rows.note: Done: the material is organised into 9 parts and 27 chapters, and Shaikhah’s notes are used in many of them.

rows.item: Shaikha and others to help collect examples and materials from books, Arabic poetry, proverbs, idioms and different text types, citing and referencing the sources
rows.note: Partly: proverbs, idioms, poetry and text types were added and cited, but the original sources of the draft’s own examples are unknown, so they are credited to the team’s course materials.

rows.item: The handbook will be used during the Guild Season, so the Translation Team can distribute it in workshops and use it with students
rows.note: Done: the Preface says “Use it in workshops or on your own”; the Guild Season is not named.

rows.item: Masooma to help with practice texts and to contribute to the practical section
rows.note: Material not received: no practice texts from Masooma were among the files.

rows.item: Loulwah to help with examples from dictionaries
rows.where: Chapter 9, Step 5; Chapter 15, Step 1; Chapter 27, Step 3
rows.note: Done: six Kuwaiti expressions with English equivalents come from the Kuwaiti expressions dictionary that Loulwah proposed.

rows.item: Seek feedback from the supervisor and Dr Amin once the first draft is complete
rows.note: A step for after the first draft; the handbook does not mention any reviewers.

rows.item: Work on the final structure: add a table of contents and decide where the glossary, introductory tips and practical sections fit
rows.where: Contents; Chapter 2; Glossary; Put it all together
rows.note: Done: a contents page, tips in Part 1 (Chapter 2), the glossary and references at the back, and a final practice page after Chapter 27.

rows.item: Discuss common grammatical and stylistic mistakes, and whether they belong at the end of each chapter or in a separate section
rows.note: Done as one section inside the revision chapter, with separate lists for English to Arabic and Arabic to English.

rows.item: Discuss the answer key and accompanying explanations
rows.where: Try it and Check your answers, every chapter
rows.note: Done: answers follow each Try it, some with a short explanation; there is no separate key at the end.

rows.item: Add references for the 180 book, the 182 course book and all other sources used
rows.note: Partly: 42 published sources are listed in APA style and the course materials are cited as the Translation Team’s notes, but the 180 and 182 books are not listed by name.

rows.item: Decide the overall approach and framework first: each member shares instructions, a proposed framework and a vision of the structure
rows.note: Followed: all four members’ instructions are in one framework document, and a first draft of the framework was written from them.

rows.item: A set of principles followed by a few examples, then further related principles with examples, logically connected and grouped into chapters
rows.note: Followed: each chapter is a short series of numbered steps, and each step gives an idea and then examples in English and Arabic.

rows.item: Exercises at the end of each chapter, based on that chapter’s material
rows.note: Followed: every chapter has Try it questions on its own material before the Remember box.

rows.item: Layout like the book Beginning Syntax (he would share the PDF)
rows.note: Followed in spirit: a contents page, short numbered steps, light pages, a small B5 page size and a build-up from zero; the model book was not among the files, so the match was not checked.

rows.item: Other members may propose their own framework and a model book
rows.note: The other three members added their own instructions and proposals in the same document.

rows.item: An outline at the beginning
rows.note: Followed: the contents list, built from the part and chapter headings, comes before the Preface.

rows.item: A list of abbreviations at the beginning
rows.note: The list is there, with Arabic equivalents, but it sits at the back of the handbook, not at the front.

rows.item: An answer key for the exercises at the end of the book
rows.where: Check your answers, in every chapter
rows.note: The answers were placed inside each chapter, some with a short explanation, and there is no separate key at the end.

rows.item: Knowledge you have learned and can paraphrase: naming the author is optional; a direct quotation or information someone else shared must be cited
rows.note: Followed: quotations and reported information carry the author and year, and ideas from published works are cited too, which is more than the rule requires.

rows.item: Text borrowed from a book must be in quotation marks with a proper citation of the author
rows.note: Followed: direct quotations are in quotation marks with author, year and page, for example Newmark (1988, p. 5) in Chapter 1 and Nida and Taber (1969, p. 12) in Chapter 10.

rows.item: No book summaries, because of copyright; contributors give fundamental principles, ideas and insights worth passing on
rows.where: Whole handbook; copyright page; Further reading
rows.note: Followed: the chapters teach principles with short examples and cite the source of each idea, and Further reading only points to five books.

rows.item: Complete democracy: equal authority and rights, and all four names appearing equally as contributors
rows.note: Partly: the handbook is credited to the Translation Team as a whole, with no names singled out, but the list of all four names is not yet in this draft.

rows.item: Instructions, frameworks and decisions are owned collectively by the four members, and the content and topics are agreed by all four
rows.note: A working rule rather than handbook text: the draft goes to all four members for agreement.

rows.item: Do not make the process overly complicated
rows.note: Followed: the handbook uses plain language and one short step at a time.

rows.item: Information repeated across the notes of all four members is important and should be kept; include first the material that appears most often
rows.note: Followed: idioms (in all four members’ notes), collocation, equivalence and terminology (in at least two) each have their own chapter.

rows.item: A topic that appears in only one member’s notes is reviewed carefully and decided case by case
rows.note: Followed: single-source topics were judged one at a time, and some were included and some left out.

rows.item: The handbook should be general, simple and suitable for beginners, not too advanced or overly detailed
rows.note: Followed: the book assumes no background, gives an example before each name, and puts the most advanced topic, films and videos, last.

rows.item: Tips: go through your Translation Principles course notes, select what helps beginners and paste it into the main shared document
rows.note: Followed: his notes became the first draft, which is the base of most chapters in Parts 1 to 5 and of Chapters 18 and 25.
